issues.legal_issue: A co-owner who knowingly builds on property while denying another co-owner’s established share cannot claim a special equity for the improvements to compel the other co-owner to take money instead of a share in the property.
material_facts: The claimant had an established one-third share in the land, and the purchaser’s father acquired the other co-owners’ interests while denying her share.
After notice of the claimant’s claim, the purchaser’s father completed buildings on the land under an agreement with a public trust.
The purchaser’s father dealt with the land as its full owner, and the earlier courts had rejected his claim for compensation for improvements.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser’s father was in the position of a trespasser with notice of the true owner’s claim and could claim no special equity based on the improvements. The decree granting partition and possession of the claimant’s share was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: A person who builds on property with notice of another’s ownership claim, while denying that claim, cannot rely on an equity based on bona fide improvements to displace the true owner’s right to a share in the property. The Court treated the asserted equity as relying on the principle underlying s. 51 of the Transfer of Property Act, but held that the circumstances negated bona fides. It also distinguished improvements made by a co-owner because the purchaser had dealt with the property as full owner. The Court relied on the earlier rejection of the improvement-compensation claim in the prior litigation; the Partition Act was mentioned by counsel but did not support the requested procedure.

rule.if: partition_proceeding and claimant_has_established_share and builder_denied_claimant_share and builder_built_with_notice_of_claim

predicates.partition_proceeding: The case is a proceeding to divide co-owned property and allot the owners’ shares.
predicates.claimant_has_established_share: A claimant’s share in the property has been established.
predicates.builder_denied_claimant_share: The person who made improvements dealt with the property as its full owner and denied the claimant’s share.
predicates.builder_built_with_notice_of_claim: The person who made improvements built on the property while aware of the claimant’s ownership claim.

issues.definition: When a partition proceeding concerns an established share and a builder denied that share while building with notice of the claim, the builder cannot use the improvements to displace the share.

issues.legal_issue: An appeal does not abate merely because some legal representatives of a deceased respondent were omitted if the appellant diligently and bona fide identifies and impleads known legal representatives who sufficiently represent the estate, absent fraud or collusion.
material_facts: The sole respondent died while the appeal was pending.
The appellants made an enquiry about her legal representatives and applied in time to bring the representatives they had identified on record.
The representatives brought on record appeared and contested the appeal.
The omitted son and daughter were identified later, and there was no allegation that the appellants had acted without diligence or bona fides, or with fraud or collusion.
issues.conclusion: The appeal had not abated because the legal representatives brought on record sufficiently represented the estate and there was no fraud or collusion.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order XXII, r. 4(1) and (3) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, an appeal does not abate where, after diligent and bona fide enquiry, the appellant brings a legal representative of the deceased respondent on record within the prescribed time, if that representative sufficiently represents the estate and there is no fraud or collusion; the decision binds the estate. The Court approved the principle stated in Kadir v. Muthukrishna Ayyar and noted its acceptance in decisions including Muhammad Zafaryab Khan v. Abdul Razzaq Khan, Jehrabi Sadullakhan Mokasi v. Bismillabi Sadruddin Kaji, Lilo Sonar v. Jhagru Sahu, Shib Dutta Singh v. Sheikh Karim Bakhsh, Abdul Baki v. R. D. Bansilal Abirchand Firm, and Mst. Umrao Begum v. Rehmat Ilahi. It distinguished The State of Punjab v. Nathu Ram and Ram Sarup v. Munshi, which concerned abatement affecting a joint and indivisible decree where no legal representative of the deceased party remained on record to represent the estate.

rule.if: appeal_pending_after_respondent_death and diligent_bona_fide_inquiry and legal_representative_added_in_time and estate_sufficiently_represented and not fraud_or_collusion

predicates.appeal_pending_after_respondent_death: An appeal is pending when a respondent dies.
predicates.diligent_bona_fide_inquiry: The appellant makes a diligent and bona fide enquiry to identify the deceased respondent’s legal representatives.
predicates.legal_representative_added_in_time: The appellant brings an identified legal representative of the deceased respondent on record within the time allowed.
predicates.estate_sufficiently_represented: The legal representative brought on record sufficiently represents the deceased respondent’s estate in the proceeding.
predicates.fraud_or_collusion: The appellant’s omission of other legal representatives involves fraud or collusion.

issues.definition: An appeal pending after a respondent’s death does not abate if the appellant diligently and bona fide investigates, timely adds a representative who sufficiently represents the estate, and has not acted fraudulently or collusively.

issues.legal_issue: Once an appellant is informed during a pending appeal that some legal representatives of a deceased respondent were omitted, the appellant must bring those representatives on record to complete the record.
material_facts: The appeal continued after the respondent’s death with some, but not all, of her legal representatives on record.
The omission of the respondent’s son and daughter was brought to the Court’s attention during the appeal, making the appellants aware of it.
The Court concluded that the appeal should fail on the merits and therefore did not adjourn it to add the omitted representatives.
issues.conclusion: Upon learning during the appeal that legal representatives had been omitted, the appellant had a duty to bring them on record so that the appeal was properly constituted. The Court did not adjourn this appeal for that purpose because it was satisfied that the appeal failed on the merits.
issues.legal_principle: Even when the timely impleading of some legal representatives prevents abatement, an appellant who is made aware during the appeal that other legal representatives were omitted must bring those others on record so the record is complete. The Court treated this as the applicable practice under Order XXII, r. 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and followed the approach reflected in the authorities it had discussed on representation of a deceased party’s estate.

predicates.appeal_pending_after_respondent_death: An appeal is pending when a respondent dies.
predicates.omitted_legal_representatives_brought_to: During the appeal, the appellant is made aware that legal representatives of the deceased respondent have not been brought on record.

issues.definition: In an appeal pending after a respondent’s death, the appellant must add omitted legal representatives when their omission is brought to the appellant’s attention.
